verses.text: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Jerusalem, and besieged it.

The Lord  gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God;  and he carried them into the land of Shinar to the house of his god: and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god.
The king spoke to Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of Israel, even of the royal offspring  and of the nobles;

youths in whom was no defect, but well-favored, and skillful in all wisdom, and endowed with knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability to stand in the king’s palace; and that he should teach them the learning and the language of the Chaldeans.
The king appointed for them a daily portion of the king’s dainties, and of the wine which he drank, and that they should be nourished three years; that at its end they should stand before the king.
Now among these were, of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
The prince of the eunuchs gave names to them: to Daniel he gave the name Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, Shadrach; and to Mishael, Meshach; and to Azariah, Abednego.

But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Now God made Daniel to find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.

The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? so would you endanger my head with the king.
Then Daniel said to the steward whom the prince of the eunuchs had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat, and water to drink.
Then let our faces be looked on before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s dainties; and as you see, deal with your servants.
So he listened to them in this matter, and proved them ten days.
At the end of ten days their faces appeared fairer, and they were fatter in flesh, than all the youths who ate of the king’s dainties.
So the steward took away their dainties, and the wine that they should drink, and gave them pulse.
Now as for these four youths, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
At the end of the days which the king had appointed for bringing them in, the prince of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar.
The king talked with them; and among them all was found no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: therefore stood they before the king.
In every matter of wisdom and understanding, concerning which the king inquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters who were in all his realm.
Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus.

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar lays siege to Jerusalem—and I've come to see how the Lord allows difficulty to come in order to prove His faithfulness. This wasn't the end of His care for His people, even when the walls fell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here's something that took me years to understand: when it says the Lord 'gave' the king into Babylon's hand, He wasn't abandoning Judah. He was orchestrating events so His remnant would learn to trust Him in exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king chooses carefully—looking for the finest youths of Israel's nobility. But the Lord had already chosen His own: Daniel and his friends were about to demonstrate something far more valuable than royal favor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king wants to fill these young men with foreign learning and a foreign tongue. I've noticed how the world still tries this—to reshape us into its image through what we consume and what we're taught to value.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's table was meant to bind them—to make them comfortable, dependent, grateful. But fidelity doesn't come from fine dainties; it comes from knowing who you belong to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four names: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah. They were far from home, stripped of rank, renamed by strangers. Yet somehow their true names—the ones the Lord knew—were the ones that would echo through eternity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: New names, new palace, new language—the exile wanted to erase who they were. But a name given by man, no matter how grand, cannot replace the name written in the Book of Life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the pivot: Daniel purposed in his heart. Long before the crisis came, before the furnace or the lions' den, he had already decided where his loyalty lay. This is where faithfulness begins—not in the fire, but in the quiet yes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God made Daniel find kindness in the eyes of a stranger—a eunuch in a foreign court. When our hearts are bended toward the Lord, He somehow works in the hearts of those around us, in ways we cannot foresee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The steward was afraid—for his own skin, naturally. I've seen how fear makes people rigid, unable to bend even a little. But sometimes all that's needed is to ask, to propose a better way, and to trust the Lord with the rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel didn't ask for much—just a steward, just a conversation. Notice how he spoke to the appointed official, not over him. Humility doesn't demand; it requests, and respects the one who must decide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten days. Such a small thing to ask—a test, plain vegetables, water. Daniel knew what he needed to prove his point wasn't pride but faithfulness. And he invited the steward to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The comparison would speak for itself—no sermon needed, just the evidence of health and strength. This is how the Spirit often works: He shows us, through our own eyes, the difference between His ways and the world's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He listened. A man in power, whose head was on the line, was willing to try something different because Daniel had asked with respect and offered to prove his case. Kindness opens doors that demands cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten days later, the evidence appeared: health and vitality. Not because vegetables are magic, but because faithfulness to the Lord carries with it a kind of wholeness the world cannot produce, even when the world is trying to make us comfortable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The steward did what we might never have dared: he changed the orders, removed the fine food, gave them pulse. He risked something for these young men—and God protected him. Sometimes our quiet faithfulness gives courage to others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gave them knowledge and skill—not in spite of their faithfulness, but as part of it. Daniel wasn't choosing between being smart and being faithful; the Lord was giving him both, because His kingdom is not divided against itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The three years came to an end, and these four youths stood where they were supposed to stand—before the most powerful man in the known world. The test wasn't whether they would be taken, but what they would become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king found in them something he didn't find in anyone else. When we stay true to the Lord, He marks us with a quality the world recognizes even when it cannot name it—the mark of a life ordered toward something real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten times better—not a little better, but overwhelmingly, undeniably superior. This is what righteousness produces when given the chance: a clarity, a wisdom, an excellence that shames all lesser things. The magicians had their tricks; Daniel had his God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daniel continued even to the first year of king Cyrus—and readers today hear an echo in that word 'continued.' He outlasted empires, stayed faithful through every reign, because his root went deeper than any throne. We too are called to continue, not in the kingdom of this age, but in His.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
